title: Woman, behold thy son (John 19:25–27)
hookLine: the disciple takes her into his own home; Catholics hear Mary given to all
carry: he took her to his own

cards: People in hospice often spend their last strength on the people they're leaving. Who'll take care of Mom? Make sure your sister's okay.

Promise me you'll call him. When everything else is slipping away, what's left is love, arranging things. Jesus has been nailed to a cross outside Jerusalem, and the soldiers are dividing his clothes at the foot of it.
John notices who else is standing there, close enough to hear. A few women. One disciple.

teach.h: AT THE FOOT OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: John names them: his mother, his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. And the disciple whom Jesus loved, never named in this Gospel, whom tradition identifies as John.

Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "When Jesus therefore had seen his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he saith to his mother: Woman, behold thy son. After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own."
Woman. It sounds cold in English. It wasn't, then; it was a respectful way to address a woman.
But it's an unusual word for a son to use with his mother, and John has had Jesus use it with her before.
At the wedding in Cana, at the very start, Jesus said to her: woman, what is that to me and to thee? My hour is not yet come. Now the hour has come, and he says woman again.
Some readers also hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis, the mother of all the living. On one level, this is a dying son making sure his mother isn't left alone. But Catholics have heard more.
The disciple stands for every disciple, so Mary is given as mother to all who follow Jesus.
Pope Paul the Sixth named her Mother of the Church during the Second Vatican Council, and Pope Francis later gave that title its own memorial, on the Monday after Pentecost.
Some Christians, especially Protestants, read the scene mainly as a son's care for his mother. And from that hour, the text says, he took her to his own.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church, on the Monday after Pentecost, and some keep an image of Mary at home and pray the Hail Mary each day.

o: take her into your own home from that hour.
bring her back to Galilee to her family.

practice: Look around the place you live for a moment, a shelf, a table, a corner, and picture welcoming someone in to stay, the way the disciple welcomed Mary.
Some Catholics keep an image of Mary somewhere at home, a small statue or a picture.
If you pray, welcome her with the words Jesus gave, behold thy mother, or pray a Hail Mary; if you don't, think of someone who needs a place, and hold them.

wordCard.voice: Woman. What Jesus calls his mother at Cana and again from the cross, giving her to the beloved disciple and him to her. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: woman, the form used to address her (John 2:4 and 19:26).
